papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) ranging from 30% to 50% have been recognized as a major threat to postoperative recovery. Current conventional interventions cannot effectively reduce the occurrence of PPCs. OBJECTIVE: In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration on PPCs in elderly patients. METHODS: In this double-blind, randomized, controlled trial, elderly patients were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to receive multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration (MD group) or normal saline nasal spray (NS group). The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs within 7 days after surgery. Key secondary outcomes included the severity grading and classification of PPCs. Other secondary outcomes included serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels, Richards-Campbell sleep questionnaire (RCSQ) scores at predefined time points, and adverse reactions. RESULTS: A total of 190 patients were screened, and 186 completed the study. The incidence of PPCs was significantly lower in the MD group than in the NS group (9.68% vs. 22.58%, P = 0.017), with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.333 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.173-6.317], absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 12.90%, and number needed to treat (NNT) of 7.75. Sensitivity analyses using the per-protocol population (PP) dataset yielded consistent results, confirming the stability and reliability of the primary outcome. The distribution of severity grading of PPCs also differed significantly between the groups (P = 0.036). After Bonferroni correction, the between-group difference in PPCs severity grading was not statistically significant (corrected P = 0.072). The distribution of pneumonia also differed significantly between the groups (P = 0.029). There were significant group effects, time effects, and interaction effects for IL-6, TNF-α, and RCSQ in the two groups after surgery (all P < 0.05). No significant between-group differences were observed in drug-related adverse events. CONCLUSION: Multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration significantly reduces the incidence of PPCs in elderly patients undergoing radical thoracoscopic lung-cancer resection with a favorable safety profile. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=243165; identifier ChiCTR2400090593.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Ciprofol is a novel intravenous anesthetic with potentially improved hemodynamic stability and fewer injection-related adverse effects than propofol. This study compared ciprofol and propofol for general anesthesia in patients undergoing video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, double-blind trial, 120 adults undergoing elective thoracoscopic surgery were randomized to ciprofol (n = 60) or propofol (n = 60). MAP, HR, and BIS were assessed at eight predefined perioperative time points using linear mixed-effects models. The repeated binary outcome of BIS ≥60 was analyzed using a generalized linear mixed-effects model. Induction characteristics, injection pain, recovery profiles, and perioperative adverse events were also evaluated. RESULTS: MAP differed significantly between groups, with higher values in the ciprofol group at loss of consciousness and after tracheal intubation. HR was modestly higher at selected early time points, without a significant group-by-time interaction. BIS was higher with ciprofol during the early intraoperative period, and BIS ≥60 was more frequent at loss of consciousness (76.7% vs. 43.3%, p < 0.001), but not thereafter. Ciprofol was associated with shorter induction time (38.3 vs. 46.0 s, p < 0.001), less injection pain (5.0% vs. 20.0%, p = 0.025), and shorter PACU stay (48.0 vs. 55.7 min, p = 0.011). No significant differences were observed in supplemental anesthetic requirements, emergence time, or perioperative adverse events. CONCLUSIONS: Ciprofol showed a perioperative profile broadly comparable to propofol, with transient differences in hemodynamic parameters and higher BIS during the early intraoperative period. Ciprofol was associated with faster induction, less injection pain, and shorter PACU stay. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=203394, Identifier: ChiCTR2400082924.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical utility of photon counting computed tomography (PCCT)-derived quantitative parameters for assessing interstitial lung disease (ILD) burden in patients with inflammatory idiopathic myopathy (IIM), comparing standard-dose (SD) and tin-filtered low-dose (LD) protocols, and to assess the added value of ultrathin reconstructions. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this single-centre prospective study (September 2023-November 2024), outpatients with IIM-ILD underwent two consecutive PCCT scans. Quantitative ILD features were extracted using a commercial deep-learning software (ContextFlow ADVANCE Chest CT). Primary analyses compared LD 1.0 mm with SD 1.0 mm reconstructions using Bland-Altman analysis, with exploratory analyses of ultrathin (0.4 mm) reconstructions. Correlation analyses between deep learning-derived quantitative parameters, visual assessment, and pulmonary function tests were performed. RESULTS: Forty-eight adults with IIM-ILD (40 females; mean age, 53.88 ± 11.13 years) were included. The LD protocol achieved a substantial dose reduction (CTDIvol: 0.77 vs 5.40 mGy) while maintaining good agreement with SD (mean net differences [MNDs] < 1% for all patterns). LD-1.0 mm protocol yielded higher volume of ground-glass opacity (MND, 0.98%) and lower volume of fibrosis extent (MND, -0.64%). Reticular pattern showed strong association with FVC% (rhoSD1.0mm = -0.62, p < 0.001) and DLCO% (rhoSD1.0mm = -0.73, p < 0.001), with similar correlations observed under LD acquisition (Δrho ≤ 0.02). Ultrathin reconstructions yielded greater measurement of bronchiectasis (MND, 0.13% on SD scans). CONCLUSION: LD PCCT serves as a radiation-sparing alternative for quantitative disease assessment. Ultrathin reconstructions provide limited additional value. Future longitudinal studies are warranted to validate the performance of LD PCCT for disease monitoring. KEY POINTS: Question Can LD photon-counting CT provide robust quantitative assessment of ILD burden in patients with inflammatory myopathy compared with SD imaging? Findings Deep learning segmentation yielded LD ILD patterns that closely matched SD results, with all MNDs below 1%. Clinical relevance LD PCCT maintains quantitative robustness and physiological validity for IIM-ILD assessment, with total disease burden showing good agreement with the SD protocol, offering a radiation-sparing alternative without compromising CT-physiology correlation.

papers.abstract_en: KRAS G12C-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has become a clinically actionable molecular subtype. Discovery of the switch-II pocket enabled the development of covalent KRAS G12C(OFF)-state inhibitors, transforming a historically "undruggable" target into a therapeutic vulnerability. Drugging KRAS, however, proved to be a problem of chemistry, whereas sustaining its inhibition has proved to be a problem of biology. KRAS G12C-mutant NSCLC is biologically heterogeneous, and the magnitude and durability of clinical benefit are shaped by co-mutations, the tumor microenvironment, brain metastases status, pharmacologic differences between agents, and the dynamic evolution of resistance. Randomized trials have demonstrated that sotorasib and adagrasib improve progression-free survival (PFS) and objective response rates (ORR) over docetaxel in previously treated disease, yet these gains have not translated consistently into a definitive overall survival (OS) advantage. This review synthesizes the epidemiology, molecular biology, diagnostic strategies, first- and later-line treatment evidence, resistance mechanisms, and emerging KRAS/RAS-directed approaches. We distinguish randomized or guideline-supported practice from early-phase and translational signals, and propose an implementable framework that combines PD-L1, tumor mutational burden, STK11/KEAP1/TP53 status, TTF-1 expression, brain metastases, and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for risk stratification and mechanism-guided management. At disease progression, oligoprogression should be distinguished from systemic progression, and tissue re-biopsy together with plasma profiling should be considered when feasible. In China, several domestically developed KRAS G12C inhibitors have been approved, and reimbursement coverage is expanding; the cost of molecular testing, uneven institutional access, regional disparities and limited confirmatory and real-world evidence nonetheless continue to constrain implementation. Future priorities include randomized first-line comparisons, biomarker-defined combination strategies, improved central nervous system activity and mechanism-matched treatment after resistance.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, and resistance to targeted therapy and immunotherapy represents a substantial unmet clinical need. Trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have emerged as a promising therapeutic class. AREAS COVERED: This drug evaluation summarizes the pharmacological rationale, molecular design, preclinical activity, clinical efficacy, safety profile, and regulatory development of sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT; MK-2870/SKB264) in NSCLC. Relevant evidence was identified through searches of PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, major oncology congress proceedings, and regulatory announcements through 20 September 2026. EXPERT OPINION: Randomized trials have demonstrated improved progression-free survival (PFS) with sac-TMT versus docetaxel and platinum-pemetrexed chemotherapy in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated advanced NSCLC after EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI) progression. In advanced NSCLC without actionable driver alterations, sac-TMT plus pembrolizumab improved PFS versus pembrolizumab alone in programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-positive disease; however, overall survival (OS) remains immature, and superiority over contemporary chemoimmunotherapy has not been established. The principal clinically relevant toxicities are hematologic toxicity and stomatitis. Future studies should clarify predictive biomarkers, optimal treatment sequencing, intracranial activity, and generalizability, while generating mature survival and quality-of-life data.

papers.abstract_en: In a cancer clinical trial with an immunotherapy, the treatment often becomes effective after a certain delay time. It is well known that traditional log-rank test no longer provides optimal power in this case. There has been a great interest to search for a more powerful test to detect a truly effective immunotherapy treatment. In this paper, we propose a new testing method based on the maximum value of a set of 0-1 weighted log-rank test statistics and establish useful theoretical results of the relevant test statistics. Extensive simulation studies are conducted to examine the empirical performance of the proposed method. An analysis of the real data from a non-small-cell lung cancer clinical trial is also carried out to further demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed test method. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT01903993, NCT02008227.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Although radiotherapy (RT) and natural killer (NK) cell-based therapy have shown promising potential in the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the therapeutic efficacy and safety of their combination remain to be fully elucidated. In this study, we evaluated the efficacy and safety of combined RT and NK cell therapy and performed preliminary proteomic profiling to characterize its potential effects on the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), providing new insights and a theoretical and clinical basis for the development of NK cell-based therapeutic strategies for NSCLC. METHODS: C57BL/6-derived subcutaneous Lewis lung carcinoma models were established to determine the minimal effective dose of both radiotherapy and adoptively transferred natural killer cells. Based on the MED-derived findings, the mice were further randomized into five experimental groups for therapeutic efficacy evaluation: the Control group, the RT group, the NK group, the combination therapy group (RN group), and the repeated combination therapy group (RN2 group). Tumour volume and body weight were monitored longitudinally. Differentially abundant proteins were interrogated by Gene Ontology enrichment and Kyoto Encyclopaedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analyses to systematically describe the synergistic antitumor efficacy of differentially expressed proteins. RESULTS: Compared with RT or NK cell-based immunotherapy as monotherapies, the RN group exhibited markedly enhanced tumor growth inhibition, with no overt treatment-related toxicities observed. Following the second cycle of combined therapy, mice in the RN2 group displayed a more pronounced reduction in tumor growth rate with those in the single-cycle combination cohort; notably, no significant adverse events associated with the combined regimen were detected throughout the entire experimental duration. Proteomic profiling unraveled that RT disrupted the core regulatory networks governing intracellular DNA replication and repair processes in tumor cells in a therapy-specific manner, whereas NK cell immunotherapy potently and selectively activated the classical pathway of the host complement system. CONCLUSION: Collectively, RT and NK cell therapy demonstrate superior synergistic efficacy and no overt toxicity was observed, with repeated treatments further delaying tumor progression. Mechanistically, proteomics shows that RT disrupts DNA replication/repair networks, whereas NK cell therapy was associated with upregulation of multiple complement components, including those belonging to the classical and lectin pathways, suggesting a potential involvement of these pathways.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: The application of segmentectomy for deep-located tumors remains controversial as the result of margin concerns. This study evaluated septum-guided segmentectomy, which uses intersegmental septa and veins as anatomical boundaries to ensure precise dissection independent of fixed linear margin requirements. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 292 patients with deep-located cT1a-bN0M0 non-small cell lung cancer undergoing septum-guided segmentectomy (n = 130) or lobectomy (n = 162) via a minimally invasive approach (January 2019 to March 2025). To rigorously control for selection bias, propensity-score matching incorporating key physiological and anatomical confounders was performed, generating 88 well-balanced matched pairs (n = 176). Perioperative outcomes, locoregional recurrence, recurrence-free survival, and overall survival were evaluated. RESULTS: After propensity-score matching, baseline balance was achieved across key covariates. Survival analysis using stratified methods revealed no significant differences in recurrence-free survival or overall survival between the groups (P> .05). Notably, despite a substantial proportion of patients in the segmentectomy group not fulfilling standard National Comprehensive Cancer Network margin criteria (>20 mm or greater tumor size)-with a mean margin distance of 14.1 mm-no locoregional recurrence was observed during follow-up. R0 resection was achieved in all patients. Although segmentectomy involved longer operative times (P< .001), perioperative complications and hospital stays were highly comparable between the 2 cohorts. CONCLUSIONS: Septum-guided segmentectomy demonstrates preliminary oncologic safety and perioperative outcomes comparable with lobectomy for deep-located early-stage non-small cell lung cancer. By using the intersegmental septum as a reliable anatomical barrier, this concept establishes a precise surgical paradigm that safely reduces the reliance on fixed margin distances.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Outcome data for the Gemini S bipolar radiofrequency clamp are almost absent; the only indexed report being a three-patient case series. We describe 1-year outcomes in a consecutive cohort. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed all consecutive patients treated with the Gemini S clamp between January 2021 and August 2024. Epicardial box isolation was combined with left atrial appendage (LAA) exclusion; completeness was confirmed by entry and exit block on epicardial three-dimensional mapping. The primary outcome was freedom from AF recurrence at 12 months, on and off antiarrhythmic drugs (AADs) after a 90-day blanking period. RESULTS: Twenty-three patients were included (mean age 64.4 ± 8.0 years; 82.6% male). AF was paroxysmal in 34.8%, persistent in 26.1%, and long-standing persistent in 39.1%; 60.9% had prior catheter ablation and 69.6% had failed or were intolerant to a Class I or III agent. A complete block-verified box lesion was achieved in 95.7% and LAA exclusion in 91.3%. Three patients (13.0%) required conversion to sternotomy for bleeding, exceeding larger series. There was no death, stroke, phrenic nerve palsy, or pacemaker implantation. At 1 year, 87.0% (95% CI 67.9-95.5) were in sinus rhythm, all off Class I/III AADs. CONCLUSIONS: Sinus rhythm was achieved in 87.0% of patients at 1 year. As the largest reported experience with this device, the series provides device-level evidence where little existed, but it is descriptive, not powered for comparison, and the conversion rate needs confirmation.

papers.abstract_en: Perioperative treatment plays an increasingly important role in improving outcomes for patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) offers a new perspective for optimizing individualized perioperative management. This review systematically examines the core value of ctDNA in perioperative therapy for resectable NSCLC, encompassing its correlation with treatment response and pathological remission during the neoadjuvant phase, its utility as a dynamic monitor of treatment efficacy, and its emerging role in prognostic stratification and recurrence prediction in the postoperative setting. Importantly, while ctDNA demonstrates considerable promise for guiding individualized perioperative management, most applications remain investigational; we therefore distinguish between established correlative uses and prospective strategies currently under evaluation in clinical trials. It also addresses current technical challenges in ctDNA application, including limited sensitivity, false positives, lack of standardization, cost-effectiveness concerns, and difficulties in integration into clinical decision-making. Future prospective interventional studies are needed to validate ctDNA-guided treatment adjustments and to establish standardized protocols and multidisciplinary collaboration pathways, thereby facilitating the integration of ctDNA into the full course of perioperative management for NSCLC and enabling precise efficacy assessment, risk stratification, and individualized treatment decisions.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether a protocolized intraoperative temperature-management strategy based on time-segmented warning thresholds and tiered, feedback-guided warming interventions reduces hypothermia and improves early postoperative recovery in patients undergoing radical esophagectomy. METHODS: This single-center retrospective comparative cohort study included 116 adults who underwent elective radical esophagectomy at The affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University between August 2024 and January 2026 and were managed with either a time-segmented, feedback-guided tiered warming protocol (n = 58) or conventional warming (n = 58). Core temperature was monitored continuously with a lower esophageal probe until the start of esophageal mobilization and with a nasopharyngeal probe thereafter, and was recorded every 15 min. All warming adjustments were implemented manually by the clinical team according to predefined thresholds. The primary endpoint was intraoperative hypothermia, defined as a core temperature below 36 °C at any time from incision to skin closure. Secondary endpoints included severe hypothermia, nadir temperature, hypothermia burden, postoperative shivering, time to extubation, post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) recovery time, coagulation indices, 30-day complications, length of stay, and hospital cost. RESULTS: Intraoperative hypothermia occurred in 53 of 58 control patients (91.4%) and 5 of 58 intervention patients (8.6%) (risk ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.04-0.22; P < 0.001). Severe hypothermia below 35.5 °C developed in 27 control patients (46.6%) and in none of the intervention patients. Median nadir core temperature was 35.55 °C in the control group and 36.27 °C in the intervention group (P < 0.001). Compared with conventional warming, the protocol reduced postoperative shivering (5.2% vs 51.7%), shortened time to extubation by 8.9 min, lowered the rate of any postoperative complication (34.5% vs 62.1%; P = 0.005), shortened hospital stay (12.2 vs 13.5 days; P = 0.010), and reduced mean in-hospital cost by 8,911 CNY (P < 0.001). The treatment effect was materially unchanged in adjusted analyses using Firth penalized logistic regression (adjusted odds ratio 0.004, 95% CI 0.000-0.024) and modified Poisson regression (adjusted risk ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.04-0.23). CONCLUSION: In adults undergoing radical esophagectomy, a time-segmented, feedback-guided tiered warming protocol substantially reduced intraoperative hypothermia and was associated with faster early recovery, fewer postoperative complications, shorter hospitalization, and lower cost. Because the intervention was a multicomponent warming bundle, the contributions of its individual components cannot be separated, and the associations with complications, hospital stay, and cost should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. The protocol uses standard perioperative equipment and can be implemented without specialized hardware.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Bacterial biofilms pose a significant healthcare challenge due to their robust resistance to antibiotics and their involvement in various diseases, including cancer and infectious conditions. Biofilms hinder the antimicrobial activity of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) by restricting their penetration through the extracellular matrix. With the rise of antimicrobial resistance, non-antibiotic strategies are gaining attention. Galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS) have been investigated for their potential to inhibit bacterial growth. This study investigates the impact of GOS on the biofilm development of GFP-labelled Staphylococcus aureus (GFP-SA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (GFP-PA) in the presence of blood PMNs from patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and healthy controls.Materials and Methods: Bacterial biofilms were investigated in the presence or absence of PMNs isolated from the blood of 12 NSCLC patients and 3 healthy controls (HC), with the inclusion of GOS. These PMNs were incubated with GFP-SA or GFP-PA biofilms and exposed to various concentrations of GOS (2.5%, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20%) for 24 hours in a microplate setting. The progress of bacterial biofilm was quantified using the crystal violet assay. RESULTS: GOS itself, with bacteria at high concentrations (10%, 15%, and 20%), suppressed biofilm formation. PMNs of NSCLC patients show higher biofilm formation than in the absence of PMNs. CONCLUSION: Based on our findings, PMNs in NSCLC patients may disrupt the natural balance of bacteria in the lungs, potentially leading to an overgrowth of biofilm-forming bacteria. GOS are known to influence immune function and may improve the ability of PMNs to fight infections. Consequently, it is proposed that GOS could enhance the ability of PMNs to phagocytose bacterial biofilms and counteract the negative effects of cancerous PMNs on biofilm formation. However, further research is needed to confirm whether GOS can effectively manage bacterial biofilms in lung cancer patients.

papers.abstract_en: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) encompasses a diverse group of histologic subtypes, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma (SqCC), and the less common but clinically aggressive adenosquamous carcinoma. Intratumoral histologic heterogeneity is a recognized challenge in NSCLC and may result in diagnostic discordance when sampling is limited. Cytologic-pathologic discordance may raise concern for tumor heterogeneity, sampling error, or misidentified histologic subtype. In such scenarios, molecular profiling and re-biopsy are essential to refine diagnosis and guide therapy. Here, we present a case of a 70-year-old man with a known history of SqCC of the lung who presented with progressive shortness of breath and was found to have a large pericardial effusion. Cytologic analysis of the pericardial fluid revealed malignant adenocarcinoma cells, discordant with the prior SqCC diagnosis. Molecular profiling of the pericardial fluid identified a TP53 mutation, intermediate tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite stability, without actionable oncogenic drivers. Repeat tissue sampling reconfirmed SqCC histology with high PD-L1 expression. The patient was initially treated with pembrolizumab monotherapy but required escalation to carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab due to disease progression. The cytologic discordance raised suspicion for unrecognized adenosquamous carcinoma or tumor heterogeneity not captured on initial biopsy. No evidence of a second primary malignancy or histologic transformation was found. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges and therapeutic implications of cytologic-pathologic discordance in NSCLC. It underscores the importance of molecular profiling and repeat tissue sampling in guiding personalized treatment decisions when histologic uncertainty exists.
